opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. I think the answer goes back to what NVIDIA has always done well, which is building the platform before the killer app fully arrives.

If you look at the history, we built CUDA and GPUs for accelerated computing, and then deep learning came along and it turned out to be the perfect workload. We built the infrastructure for the AI wave before most people realized how big it would be. I see robotics the same way. Physical AI, meaning intelligence that can actually act in the world, is the next big frontier after language models and digital agents. Humanoids in particular are interesting because the world is built around the human form. Our factories, homes, kitchens, and tools are all designed for human hands and bodies. If you can build a general-purpose humanoid, you can in principle deploy it anywhere a human can work, without redesigning the environment.

The problem is that robotics today is very fragmented. Every company builds its own stack, collects its own little dataset, and trains models that are very specialized. It feels like where computer vision or NLP was before foundation models. Nobody has really cracked the "GPT moment" for robotics yet, and part of the reason is that the whole pipeline is so hard to put together.

So I think about it as three computers. First, you need a computer to train the brain: large-scale GPU clusters to train robot foundation models. Second, you need a computer to simulate the world. Robotics has a big data problem. You can't scrape robot actions off the internet like you can scrape text. So simulation becomes essential: you generate huge amounts of synthetic experience and train robots in a sort of "matrix" before you put them in the real world. Third, you need a computer that sits on the robot itself, running the model in real time with tight power and latency constraints.

NVIDIA is in a unique position to provide all three, along with the software that connects them: simulation, synthetic data generation, foundation models, and onboard compute. Our goal isn't to build every robot ourselves. We want to be the platform that lets every robotics company, whatever body they're building, move much faster. If we do that well, I think we'll look back and see this as the moment robotics went from bespoke engineering projects to something that scales like the rest of AI.

So for me the "why NVIDIA" question kind of answers itself. Everything that moves will eventually be autonomous, and someone has to build the foundation that makes that possible. We'd love for it to be us.

r001.rationale: The response describes NVIDIA’s platform as combining simulation, foundation models, GPU training clusters, and onboard robot compute.

r002.rationale: It explicitly predicts that “everything that moves will eventually be autonomous.”

r003.rationale: It argues for building the platform ahead of robotics’ arrival, but does not mention robots becoming as numerous as iPhones or use that prospect to justify starting now.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the easiest way to put it is that Nvidia has always been a company that builds platforms for whatever the next big wave of computing is, and I believe physical AI is that next wave. We've had the GPU for graphics, then the GPU for deep learning, and now large language models. And I think the natural progression is that intelligence has to leave the screen and go into the physical world. Robots are the embodiment of that.

The reason I'm so focused on humanoids specifically is that the world is built for humans. Our doors, our stairs, our kitchens, our factories, our tools, everything is designed around the human form. So if you want a single robot form factor that can plug into the maximum number of environments without having to redesign the world, the humanoid is the obvious answer. And once you have that form factor, you need a brain to drive it, and that brain is a foundation model for robotics.

And this is where the platform argument comes in. Training these models is not just about scraping the internet. For robots, the data doesn't exist in the same abundance. You can't just download a trillion tokens of robot actions. So you need simulation. You need to generate the data in a virtual world, at scale, with physics that are accurate enough to transfer to reality. That is a massive compute problem, it's a graphics problem, and it's an AI problem all at once. Nvidia happens to be the one company that sits at the intersection of all three. We have the GPUs, we have the simulation stack with Omniverse and Isaac, and we have the deep learning expertise.

So the way I think about it, there are really three computers involved. There's the computer that trains the model, which is the big data center. There's the computer that runs the simulation to generate the data and test the policies. And then there's the computer that lives on the robot itself, running inference in real time on a tight power budget. If one company can provide a coherent platform across all three, that dramatically lowers the barrier for everyone else trying to build robots. That's what we did for the LLM ecosystem, and I think we can do it again for the physical world.

And honestly, I think the opportunity is bigger. Language models automate digital labor. Robots automate physical labor, which is a much larger slice of the global economy. So if you believe that embodied intelligence is coming, and I very much do, then building the platform for it is not a side project. It's the next chapter of the company.

r001.rationale: The response presents a robotics platform combining Nvidia GPUs, a robotics foundation model, and simulation through Omniverse and Isaac.

r002.rationale: It predicts that intelligence will enter the physical world, but does not say that everything that moves will eventually be autonomous.

r003.rationale: It argues that robotics is a major opportunity and that building a platform is the next chapter, but does not claim robots could be as numerous as iPhones or use that prospect to justify starting now.

astra-6.text:
I think robotics is one of the most compelling next frontiers for computing. If we can build intelligence that operates in the physical world, then computers can help us with a much broader range of tasks than they can through a screen. But getting there requires much more than a good model. You need a whole computing platform.

You need compute to train the models, simulation to give robots experience, and onboard compute to run those models in real time. Those pieces have to work together. A robot needs to perceive its surroundings, reason about what to do, and control its body—and it has to do that under the constraints of the physical world.

Nvidia is in a strong position to build that infrastructure because the problem brings together AI, graphics, and accelerated computing. Simulation is particularly important: you can’t scale robot learning by having people supervise every attempt on a physical robot. You need a way to practice across many environments and conditions, then transfer what the robot learns into the real world.

The goal is to give robot builders a shared foundation. Different companies will build different bodies and focus on different applications. If we can provide the computing platform underneath them, we can help that entire ecosystem move faster.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a shared platform combining training and onboard compute, models, and simulation.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses robotics as a frontier but does not predict that everything that moves will become autonomous.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not compare robots to iPhones in number or argue that this prospect makes building the platform urgent now.

sol-6.1.text:
I think robotics is one of the next great computing platforms. If you want AI to do useful work in the physical world, intelligence alone isn’t enough. You need a whole stack: compute on the robot, infrastructure to train the models, and simulation to let those models practice before you deploy them.

That’s a very natural role for Nvidia. We shouldn’t have to build every robot ourselves. We can build the computing platform that enables lots of different companies to build robots, whether they’re humanoids, robot arms, or something else entirely.

Humanoids are particularly interesting because we’ve designed our world around the human body. But the broader opportunity is physical intelligence: getting machines to perceive, reason, and act in that world. A shared platform means each team doesn’t have to reinvent all the infrastructure before it can start solving useful problems.

r001.rationale: The response describes on-robot compute, model-training infrastructure, and simulation, but does not clearly identify chips and foundation models as parts of the platform.

r002.rationale: It does not predict that everything that moves will eventually be autonomous.

r003.rationale: It does not mention robots becoming as numerous as iPhones or use that prospect to argue for building the platform now.
